$x=$.................... , $y=$....................  
$x=$.................... , $y=$....................
parts.solutionMd:
> *This question says 'you must show all your working', so show a clear algebraic method and then check on your calculator*

> *Number the equations*

$\begin{gathered} y = 4 - x \\ x^{2} + 2 y^{2} & = 67 \end{gathered}$ $( 1 )
( 2 )$

> *Using equation (1) substitute the linear expression (4-**x**) for **y **in equation (2)*

> *Make sure you use brackets around the expression*

$x^{2} + 2 ( 4 - x )^{2} = 67$

**[1]**

> *Expand (4-**x**)*<sup>*2 *</sup>*by writing (4-**x**)(4-**x**) and simplify*

$( 4 - x ) ( 4 - x ) = 16 - 4 x - 4 x + x^{2} = 16 - 8 x + x^{2}$

**[1]**

> *Use this expanded expression in the equation*

$x^{2} + 2 ( 16 - 8 x + x^{2} ) = 67$

> *Expand and simplify*

$x^{2}+32-16x+2x^{2}=67\,3x^{2}-16x+32=67$

> *Form a quadratic equation equal to zero by subtracting 67 from both sides*

$3x^{2}-16x-35=0$

**[1]**

> *Check to see if the quadratic can be factorised into the form *$( 3 x \pm p ) ( x \pm q )$* where **p **and **q **are factors of 35 so are 1, 5, 7 or 35, you might be able to spot this by inspection *

> *Otherwise, find a pair of numbers which add to make **b** (-16) and multiply to give **ac** (3×-21= -105)*

$\begin{gathered} - 21 + 5 & = - 16 \\ - 21 \times 5 & = - 105 \end{gathered}$

> *Write -16**x** as -21**x** + 5**x **and factorise the quadratic*

$\begin{gathered} 3 x^{2} - 16 x - 35 & = 3 x^{2} - 21 x + 5 x - 35 \\ = 3 x ( x - 7 ) + 5 ( x - 7 ) \\ = ( 3 x + 5 ) ( x - 7 ) \end{gathered}$

$\therefore ( 3 x + 5 ) ( x - 7 ) = 0$

**[1]**

> *Solve the quadratic by making each factor equal to zero*

$\begin{array}{rcl} 3 x + 5 & = 0 \Leftrightarrow x = - \frac{5}{3} \\ x - 7 & = 0 \Leftrightarrow x = 7 \end{array}$

**[1]**

> *For each **x**-value substitute back into equation (1) to find the corresponding **y**-value*

$\begin{array}{rcl} x = - \frac{5}{3} \Leftrightarrow y = 4 - ( - \frac{5}{3} ) = \frac{17}{3} \\ y = 7 \Leftrightarrow y = 4 - ( 7 ) = - 3 \end{array}$

$x=-\frac{5}{3},y=\frac{17}{3}$

**      **$x=7,y=-3$ **[1]**
** Alternative methods for solving a quadratic equation are acceptable as long as all working is shown**

parts.problemMd:
Marco is making patterns with grey and white circular mats.

![cie-igcse-2018-may-jun-1-p4-q12](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-maths-international-maths-23-extended/algebra-and-sequences/simultaneous-equations/assets/001-cie-igcse-2018-may-jun-1-p4-q12.png)

The patterns form a sequence. Marco makes a table to show some information about the patterns.

| Pattern number | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Number of grey mats | 6 | 9 | 12 | 15 |
| Total number of mats | 6 | 10 | 15 | 21 |

Marco needs a total of 6 mats to make the first pattern. 
He needs a total of 16 mats to make the first two patterns. 
He needs a total of $\frac{1}{6}n^{3}+an^{2}+bn$ mats to make the first $n$ patterns.

Find the value of $a$ and the value of $b$.

$a=$......................................... 
 $b=$.........................................
parts.solutionMd:
> $n$* is the pattern number*
*So for the first pattern, *$n=1$* and the total number of mats needed is 6*

$\frac{1}{6} ( 1 )^{3} + a ( 1 )^{2} + b ( 1 ) = 6 \textcircled{1}$

**substituting 1 into the formula **** [1]**
**equating the the formula to 6 **** [1]**

> *For the second pattern, *$n=2$* and the total number of mats needed is 16*

$\frac{1}{6} ( 2 )^{3} + a ( 2 )^{2} + b ( 2 ) = 16 \textcircled{2}$

**substituting 2 into the formula and equating to 16 **** [1]**

*We now have a pair of simultaneous equations* 
*First, expand the brackets and subtract the constant from the left hand sides, to get the equations into a format we are familiar with*

$\begin{gathered} \textcircled{1} : \frac{1}{6} + a + b & = 6 \\ a + b & = 5 \frac{5}{6} \end{gathered}$

$\begin{gathered} \textcircled{2} : \frac{8}{6} + 4 a + 2 b & = 16 \\ \frac{4}{3} + 4 a + 2 b & = 16 \\ 4 a + 2 b & = 14 \frac{2}{3} \end{gathered}$

> *Now solve by elimination *

> *It's simplest to eliminate *$b$* first*

$\begin{gathered} a + b & = 5 \frac{5}{6} \textcircled{1} \\ 4 a + 2 b & = 14 \frac{2}{3} \textcircled{2} \\ \textcircled{1} \\times 2 : 2 a + 2 b & = 11 \frac{2}{3} \textcircled{3} \\ \textcircled{2} - \textcircled{3} : 2 a & = 3 \\ \end{gathered}$

**eliminating **$a$** or **$b$** [1]**

$a=\frac{3}{2}$** [1]**

> *Substitute this value of *$a$* into equation *$\textcircled{1}  $* and solve for *$b$

$\begin{array}{ccc}\frac{3}{2} + b & = & 5 \frac{5}{6}\end{array}$

$\begin{array}{cc} b = & 4 \frac{1}{ } 3 or \frac{13}{ } 3\end{array}$** [1]**

> *Find the points where the graphs intersect by forming an equation by making the expressions equal.*

$( x - 1 )^{2} = 1 \frac{1}{2} x + 1$

**[1]**

> *Expand and simplify the left hand side by expanding *$( x - 1 ) ( x - 1 ).$

$x^{2}-x-x+1=\frac{1}{2}x+1\,x^{2}-2x+1=\frac{1}{2}x+1$

**[1]**

> *Subtract 1 from both sides.*

$x^{2}-2x=\frac{1}{2}x$

> *Subtract *$\frac{1}{2}x$* from both sides.*

$\begin{array}{rcl} x^{2} - 2 x - 1 \frac{1}{2} x & = 0 \\ x^{2} - \frac{5}{2} x & = 0 \end{array}$

**[1]**

> *Factorise out the **x**.*

$x ( x - \frac{5}{2} ) = 0$

> *Make each factor equal to zero and solve for **x**.*

$\begin{gathered} x = 0 \\ x - \frac{5}{2} & = 0 \Leftrightarrow x = \frac{5}{2} \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

> *Find the corresponding **y**-values by substitute the **x**-values into an equation for one of the graphs.*

$\begin{gathered} x = 0 \Leftrightarrow y = ( 0 - 1 )^{2} = 1 \\ x = \frac{5}{2} \Leftrightarrow y = ( \frac{5}{2} - 1 )^{2} = \frac{9}{4} \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

> *Write down the coordinates for the two points of intersection.*

`A ( 0 , 1 ) and B ( 5 / 2 , ( 9)/(4) )`

> *Find the distance between the two points using the formula *$d = \sqrt{( x_{2} - x_{1} )^{2} + ( y_{2} - y_{1} )^{2}} .$

`| d = sqrt( ( 5 / 2 - 0 ) ^2 + ( 9 / 4 - 1 ) ^2 ) | | _ = sqrt( 125 / 16 ) | | _ = (5 sqrt( 5)/(4) | | _ = 2.795084... | |`

**[1]**

> *Round to 3 significant figures.*

**AB**** = 2.80** **[1]**

$2=\frac{y-(0)}{x-0}=\frac{y}{x}$

> *Rearrange to find an expression for **y **in terms of **x.*

$y=2x$

$\begin{gathered} x^{2} & = \frac{2645}{5} = 529 \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

> *Square root both sides to find **x**.*

parts.problemMd:
The graph with equation $y=x^{2}+ax+b$  undergoes a translation of two units in the positive $x$ direction and four units in the negative $y$ direction.

The equation of the translated graph is $y=x^{2}-x-10.$

Find the values of $a$ and $b$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Method 1*

> *The easiest method is to consider the translation in reverse*
*A translation of a graph two units to the right and four units down can be reversed by translating it four units up and two units to the left *

> *Consider translating  *$y=x^{2}-x-10$*  four units up and two units to the left *

> *A translation of a graph *$f(x)$* four units up will be *$f(x)+4$

> *Add 4 to the equation of the translated graph*

$\begin{gathered} y = x^{2} - x - 10 + 4 \\ = x^{2} - x - 6 \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

> *A translation of a graph *$f(x)$* two units to the left will be *$f(x+2)$

> *Replace both *$x$*'s with *$x+2$* in the new equation of the translated graph  *

$y = ( x + 2 )^{2} - ( x + 2 ) - 6$

**[1]**

> *Expand the double brackets and simplify*

$\begin{gathered} y = ( x + 2 ) ( x + 2 ) - ( x + 2 ) - 6 \\ = ( x^{2} + 2 x + 2 x + 4 ) - ( x + 2 ) - 6 \\ = x^{2} + 4 x + 4 - ( x + 2 ) - 6 \\ = x^{2} + 4 x - 2 - ( x + 2 ) \end{gathered}$

> *Expand the single brackets and simplify*

$\begin{gathered} y = x^{2} + 4 x - 2 - x - 2 \\ = x^{2} + 3 x - 4 \end{gathered}$

> *Compare the *$x$* coefficients*

$a=3$

> *Compare the constant terms*

$b=-4$

$a=3,b=-4$** ****[1]**

> *Method 2*

> *A translation of a graph *$f(x)$* two units to the right will be *$f(x-2)$

> *Replace both *$x$*'s with *$x-2$* in the equation of the graph *

$y = ( x - 2 )^{2} + a ( x - 2 ) + b$

**[1]**

> *A translation of a graph *$f(x)$* four units downwards will be *$f(x)-4$

> *Subtract 4 from the equation of the graph *

$y = ( x - 2 )^{2} + a ( x - 2 ) + b - 4$

**[1]**

> *Expand the double brackets and simplify*

$\begin{gathered} y = ( x - 2 ) ( x - 2 ) + a ( x - 2 ) + b - 4 \\ = ( x^{2} - 2 x - 2 x + 4 ) + a ( x - 2 ) + b - 4 \\ = x^{2} - 4 x + 4 + a ( x - 2 ) + b - 4 \\ = x^{2} - 4 x + a ( x - 2 ) + b \end{gathered}$

> *Expand the single brackets*

$\begin{gathered} y = x^{2} - 4 x + a x - 2 a + b \end{gathered}$

> *Collect like terms*

$y = x^{2} + ( a - 4 ) x + ( b - 2 a )$

> *Compare the *$x$* coefficients*

$a-4=-1$

> *Solve for *$a$* *

$\begin{gathered} a = - 1 + 4 \\ a = 3 \end{gathered}$

> *Compare the constant terms*

$b-2a=-10$

> *Substitute in your value of *$a$* *

$b - 2 ( 3 ) = - 10$

> *Solve for *$b$* *

$\begin{gathered} b - 6 & = - 10 \\ b = - 10 + 6 \end{gathered}$

$a=3,b=-4$** ****[1]**

parts.solutionMd:
> *This is a quadratic function so will be the shape of a parabola (∪)*

> *You need to find where the graph crosses the coordinate axes*

> *The graph crosses the **y**-axis when **x **= 0*

$x = 0 \Leftrightarrow y = ( 0 - 3 )^{2} - 5 = 9 - 5 = 4$

> *So the graph crosses the **y **axis at the point (0, 4)*

**[1]**

> *The graph crosses the **x**-axis when **y **= 0*

$y = 0 \Leftrightarrow 0 = ( x - 3 )^{2} - 5$

> *Add 5 to both sides*

$\begin{gathered} ( x - 3 )^{2} & = 5 \end{gathered}$

> *Square root both sides and then add 3 to both sides*

$\begin{gathered} x - 3 & = \pm \sqrt{5} \\ x = 3 \pm \sqrt{5} \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

> *The graph goes through the **x **axis twice, at the points *$(3+\sqrt{5},0)$* and *$(3-\sqrt{5},0)$

> *The turning point of *$a ( x + b )^{2} + c$*is at the point *$(-b,c)$

$a = 1 , b = - 3 , c = - 5 \Leftrightarrow \text{Minimum} \text{point} : ( 3 , - 5 )$

**[1]**

> *Draw the parabola by drawing a symmetrical ∪ shape which goes through *$(0,4)$*, crosses through *$(3+\sqrt{5},0)$* and *$(3-\sqrt{5},0)$* and has a minimum point at *$(3,-5)$

parts.solutionMd:
> *This is a quadratic function so will be the shape of a parabola (∪)*

> *You need to find where the graph crosses the coordinate axes*

> *The graph crosses the **y**-axis when **x **= 0*

> *We know that **a  **> 4, so the graph crosses the **y **axis **below **zero *

> *The graph crosses the **x**-axis when **y **= 0*

$y = 0 \Leftrightarrow 0 = 4 ( x - 1 )^{2} - a$

> *Add **a** to both sides and divide by 4*

$\begin{gathered} 4 ( x - 1 )^{2} & = a \\ ( x - 1 )^{2} & = \frac{a}{4} \end{gathered}$

> *Square root both sides and then add 1 to both sides*

$\begin{array}{ccc}x - 1 & = & \pm \sqrt{\frac{a}{4}} \\ x = & 1 \pm \sqrt{\frac{a}{4}}\end{array}$

> *We know that **a  **> 4, so both answers are possible and the graph goes through the **x **axis twice*

> *The turning point of *$a ( x + b )^{2} + c$*is at the point *$(-b,c)$

$a = 4 , b = - 1 , c = - a \Leftrightarrow \text{Minimum} \text{point} : ( 1 , - a )$

> *We know that **a  **> 4, so -**a **< -4 and the minimum point must be in the fourth quadrant*

> *Draw the parabola by drawing a symmetrical ∪ shape which goes through *$(0,4-a)$*, crosses through *$(1-\sqrt{\frac{a}{4}},0)$* and *$(1+\sqrt{\frac{a}{4}},0)$* and has a minimum point at *$(1,-a)$

The separate parts of the curve y=1+2^x to the left of (-1.69, 1.31)  and to the right of (2,5) are shaded.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-maths-international-maths-23-extended/coordinate-geometry-and-graphs/using-calculators-for-graphs-equations-and-inequalities/assets/008-graph-with-curves-y-1-2-x-and-y-x-3-intersecting.png)

> *State the two separate ranges of *$x$* values*

$x<-1.69\mathrm{or}x>2$

parts.problemMd:
The solutions in part (b) are also solutions to the equation below, where $p$ and $q$ are positive integers.

$x = log_{p} ( x + q )$

Find $p$ and $q$.
parts.solutionMd:
**Method 1**

> *The solutions to part (b) satisfy the equation*

$1+2^{x}=x+3$

> *Rearrange this equation to make the *$x$* in *$2^{x}$* the subject*

$\begin{gathered} 2^{x} & = x + 3 - 1 \\ 2^{x} & = x + 2 \end{gathered}$

> *To make *$x$*the subject, use the relationship that *$a^{x}=y$* can be rewritten as *$\mathrm{log}_{a}y=x$

$x = log_{2} ( x + 2 )$

> *This is now in the form *$x = log_{p} ( x + q )$

$p=2\mathrm{and}q=2$

**[B1 B1]**

**Method 2**

> *Start from the given equation *$x = log_{p} ( x + q )$* and use that *$\mathrm{log}_{a}y=x$* can be rewritten as *$a^{x}=y$

$p^{x}=x+q$

> *Compare this to *$1+2^{x}=x+3$* from part (b) to spot the values of *$p$* and *$q$

> *It helps to add 1 to both sides of the equation*

$1+p^{x}=x+q+1$

> *Now compare this to *$1+2^{x}=x+3$

> *The *$p$* must be a 2 *

$p=2$

> *and the *$q+1$* must equal 3*

$q+1=3$

> *Solve this equation for *$q$

$q=2$

> *Present both answers*

$p=2\mathrm{and}q=2$

**[B1 B1]**

parts.problemMd: Calculate the size of one interior angle of a regular polygon with 40 sides.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Method 1*

> *The sum of the angles in a polygon with *$n$* sides is given by the  formula *$180(n-2)$*.*

> *Substitute *$n=40$* into the formula to find the sum of the angles in the polygon.*

$180(40-2)=180\times38=6840$

> *Every angle in a regular polygon is equal.*

> *Divide the sum of the angles by the number of sides to find an individual angle.*

$\frac{6840}{40}$

**[1]**

$171^{\circ}$** ****[1]**

> *Method 2*

*Exterior angles of a polygon with any number of sides always add up to 360*<sup>*°*</sup>*.* 
*Exterior angles of a regular polygon are equal.*

> *Find the size of one exterior angle of the polygon by dividing 360° by 40.*

$\frac{360}{40}=9$

> *An interior and exterior angle will add up to 180°*<sup>*  *</sup>*because they lie on a straight line.*

> *Find the size of an interior angle by subtracting the exterior angle from 180°.*

$180-9$

** [1]**

$171^{\circ}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd: Find the interior angle of a regular polygon with 24 sides.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Method 1*

> *The formula for the interior angle of an *$n$*-sided **regular** polygon is *$\frac{(n-2)\times180}{n}$*.*

$\frac{(24-2)\times180}{24}=\frac{22\times180}{24}=\frac{3960}{24}=165$

**[1]**

**165°** **[1]**

> *Method 2*

> *In any polygon, the total of all the exterior angles is 360°. *
*In a **regular** polygon, all exterior angles are equal.*

*Exterior angle** *$=\frac{360}{24}=15$

> *Now use the fact that an interior and exterior angle add up to 180°.*

$180-15=165$

**[1]**

**Final answer:** **165°**** [1]**

parts.problemMd:
The interior angle of a regular polygon with $n$ sides is 150°.

Calculate the value of $n$.

$n=$................................................
parts.solutionMd:
> *Method 1*

> *It is a regular polygon so all the interior angles are equal and all the exterior angles are equal.*

> *An interior angle and an exterior angle add up to 180°. Use this to find the size of an exterior angle.*

$\begin{gathered} 150^{\circ} + \text{Exterior} \text{angle} & = 180^{\circ} \\ \text{Exterior} \text{angle} & = 180^{\circ} - 150^{\circ} \\ \text{Exterior} \text{angle} & = 30^{\circ} \end{gathered}$

> *The formula for the exterior angle of a regular **n**-sided polygon is *$\mathrm{Exterior} \mathrm{angle}=\frac{360}{n}.$* Use this to form an equation.*

$30=\frac{360}{n}$

**[1]**

> *Multiply both sides by **n**.*

$30n=360$

> *Divide both sides by 30.*

$n=\frac{360}{30}$

$n=12$ **[1]**

> *Method 2*

> *The formula for the interior angle of a regular **n**-sided polygon is *$\text{Interior} \text{angle} = \frac{( n - 2 ) \times 180}{n} .$* Use this to form an equation.*

$150 = \frac{( n - 2 ) \times 180}{n}$

**[1]**

> *Multiply both sides by **n**.*

$150 n = ( n - 2 ) \times 180$

> *Expand the bracket.*

$150n=180n-360$

> *Subtract 180**n** from both sides.*

$\begin{array}{rcl} 150 n - 180 n & = - 360 \\ - 30 n & = - 360 \end{array}$

> *Divide both sides by -30.*

$n=\frac{-360}{-30}$

$n=12$* ***[1]**

> *This means that angle *$OMB$* is 90°*

> *Drawing a line from *$O$* to *$B$* also forms a radius, of length 12 cm*

*The internal angles of a pentagon are 108° (as found in part a), and the line *$OB$* would bisect this angle (cut it in half), due to the symmetry of the regular pentagon* 
*This means angle *$OBM$* is 54°*

![vQG17z~-_cie-igcse-2019-may-jun-p4-tz2-q7b-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-maths-international-maths-23-extended/geometry/angles-in-polygons-and-parallel-lines/assets/011-vqg17z-cie-igcse-2019-may-jun-p4-tz2-q7b-1.png)

**[1]**

> *Considering the right-angled triangle *$OMB$*, we can use the cosine ratio, *$\mathrm{cos}θ=\frac{\mathrm{adjacent}}{\mathrm{hypotenuse}}$*, to find *$BM$

$\begin{gathered} \cos ( 54 ) & = \frac{B M}{12} \\ 12 \cos ( 54 ) & = B M \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

$BM=7.053423028...$

$BM=7.05\mathrm{cm}$ **[1]**
* Rounded to 3 significant figures*

iia) *For the same reasons as for angle *$OMB$* in part i, angle *$BMX$* is also 90°*

> *As the line *$ABX$* is a straight line, we can use the fact that angles on a straight line sum to 180° at point B*

$180-54-54=72$

> *So angle *$MBX$* is 72°*

![cie-igcse-2019-may-jun-p4-tz2-q7b-2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-maths-international-maths-23-extended/geometry/angles-in-polygons-and-parallel-lines/assets/012-cie-igcse-2019-may-jun-p4-tz2-q7b-2.png)

> *Considering the right-angled triangle *$BMX$*, we can use the cosine ratio, *$\mathrm{cos}θ=\frac{\mathrm{adjacent}}{\mathrm{hypotenuse}}$*, to find length *$BX$

$\cos ( 72 ) = \frac{7.05}{B X}$

> *Multiply both sides by *$BX$*, and then divide both sides by *$\cos ( 72 )$

$B X = \frac{7.05}{\cos ( 72 )}$

**[2]**

$BX=22.81427924...$

$BX=22.8\mathrm{cm}$ **[1]** 
*Rounded to 3 significant figures*

iib) *To find the area of a non-right-angled triangle, we can use the formula:* $\mathrm{Area}=\frac{1}{2}ab\mathrm{sin}C$* where side lengths *$a$* and *$b$* are either side of angle *$C$

> *Considering triangle *$AOX$*, side length *$OA$* is 12 cm as it is the radius of the circle, and angle *$OAB$* is 54° as it is half the internal angle of the pentagon*

> *To be able to use the above formula, we still need to find the length *$AX$

![cie-igcse-2019-may-jun-p4-tz2-q7b-3](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-maths-international-maths-23-extended/geometry/angles-in-polygons-and-parallel-lines/assets/013-cie-igcse-2019-may-jun-p4-tz2-q7b-3.png)

> *To find *$AX$*, we will find *$AB$*, and then add it on to *$BX$* (which was found to be 22.8 cm in the previous part)*

> *To find *$AB$*, we can find half its length (*$AZ$*) by considering the right-angled triangle *$AZO$* and using the cosine ratio; *$\mathrm{cosθ}=\frac{\mathrm{adjacent}}{\mathrm{hypotenuse}}$

$\cos ( 54 ) = \frac{A Z}{12}$

> *Multiply both sides by 12*

$12 \cos ( 54 ) = A Z$

$AZ=7.05...$

*Finding length *$AX$* (and noting that *$ZB$* is the same length as *$AZ$*)* *Use the unrounded forms of the lengths where you can to maintain accuracy*

$AX=7.05...+7.05...+22.8=36.9...$

> *Now we can find the area of the triangle *$AOX$* using the formula *$\frac{1}{2}ab\mathrm{sin}C$

$1 \frac{1}{2} \times 12 \times 36.9... \times \sin ( 54 ) = 179.1...$

* 1 mark for correct strategy to find overall area*** [2]**
$179\mathrm{cm}^{2}$ **[1]** 
**Rounded to 3 significant figures**

> *Consider the 5-sided polygon **AGHIJ**. Find the sum of the angles using the formula: *$Sum of Interior Angle = ( n - 2 ) \times 180 ^{\circ} .$

$\begin{array}{rcl} x + x + 144 + 144 + 144 & = 540 \\ 2 x + 432 & = 540 \\ 2 x & = 108 \\ x = 54 \end{array}$

**[1]**

> *Consider the quadrilateral **ABCD**. The angles should add up to 360°. The angle at **A** is the same as the angle at **D** by symmetry. The other three angles are 144°. Form an equation and solve it to find **t**he missing angles.*

![angles-vhq6-2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-maths-international-maths-23-extended/geometry/angles-in-polygons-and-parallel-lines/assets/017-angles-vhq6-2.png)

$\begin{array}{rcl} z + z + 144 + 144 & = 360 \\ 2 z + 288 & = 360 \\ 2 z & = 72 \\ z = 36 \end{array}$

**[1]**

$\begin{array}{rcl} 54 + y + 36 & = 144 \\ y + 90 & = 144 \\ y = 54 \end{array}$

$x=y=54$* ***[1]**

parts.solutionMd:
> *The alternate segment theorem states that an angle inside a triangle with all three vertices on the circumference of a circle is equal to the angle between the opposite side and a tangent.*

> *The angle *$v$* is between a tangent and a side of two triangles which both have all three vertices on the circumference. So it is equal to both of the angles in the triangles opposite that side.*

![cie-igcse-2020-oct-nov-p4-tz2-q8a-working](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-maths-international-maths-23-extended/geometry/circle-theorems/assets/048-cie-igcse-2020-oct-nov-p4-tz2-q8a-working.png)

> $v^{\circ}=x^{\circ}=40^{\circ}$*  *

> *EC **= **EB  **so triangle** BCE **is isosceles and angle **CBE** = angle **BCE**. *

$\begin{gathered} w^{\circ} & = 80^{\circ} \end{gathered}$

> *ABCE **is a cyclic quadrilateral. This theorem states that opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180°.*

$\begin{gathered} y + 80 & = 180 \\ y & = 180 - 80 \\ y^{\circ} & = 100^{\circ} \end{gathered}$

> *BCDE **is also a cyclic quadrilateral. *

*A*, *B*, *C* and *D* are points on the circle, centre *O*. 
Angle *ABD* = 21° and *CD* = 12 cm.

Calculate the area of the circle.

.......................................... cm<sup>2</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
> *The area of a circle is π**r*<sup>*2*</sup>*, so the radius of the circle is needed.*

> *AC **is a diameter** **of the circle and so triangle** ACD **is a triangle formed by a semicircle with all three vertices at the circumference. The circle theorem 'the angle in a semicircle is always a right angle' states that the angle **ADC **must be a right angle.*

*Angle ***ADC  ***= 90°*

** ****[1]**

> *ABD **and **ACD **are both angles subtended from the same arc, so by the circle theorem 'the angles in the same segment are equal',*

*Angle ***ACD  ***= angle ***ABD ***= 21°.*

** ****[1]**

> *ACD ** is a right-angled triangle so right-angled trigonometry (SOHCAHTOA) can be used to find the diameter of the circle, **AC**.*
*AC **is the hypotenuse, the angle and the side adjacent to it are known, so use the cos ratio.  *

$\mathrm{cos}θ=\frac{\mathrm{Adj}}{\mathrm{Hyp}}\,\mathrm{cos}21^{\circ}=\frac{12}{AC}$

**[1]**

> *Solve by multiplying both sides by **AC **and dividing both sides by 12.   *

$\begin{gathered} A C \cos 21^{\circ} & = 12 \\ A C & = \frac{12}{\cos 21^{\circ}} \\ = 12.85373... \end{gathered}$

*   ***[1]**

> *The radius is half the diameter.*

$\begin{array}{rcl} r & = \frac{12.85373...}{2} = 6.42686... \end{array}$

> *Substitute into the formula for the area of a circle.*

$\begin{gathered} \mathrm{\pi } ( 6.42686... )^{2} & = 129.7624.... \end{gathered}$

* ***Area = 130 cm**<sup>**2**</sup>** (3 s.f.) ****[1]**
**If not rounded to 3 s.f., answers in the range 129.6 to 129.8 accepted.*** *

parts.problemMd:
![q5-4-4-very-hard-edexcel-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-maths-international-maths-23-extended/geometry/circle-theorems/assets/003-q5-4-4-very-hard-edexcel-gcse-maths.png)

$PQRST$ is a regular pentagon.
$R,U$ and $T$ are points on a circle, centre $O$.
$QR$ and $PT$ are tangents to the circle.
$RSU$ is a straight line.

Prove that $ST=UT$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *To prove that **ST  **is equal to** UT ** you will need to **prove **that the triangle **STU **is **isosceles**. This can be done by finding the angles. *

> *PQRST **is a regular pentagon, so the angle **TSU** is the exterior angle of a regular pentagon. *
*Exterior angles in any polygon add up to 360°.*
*A regular pentagon has 5 equal exterior angles.*

> * *$T \hat{S} U = \frac{360}{5} = 72^{\circ}$

**[1]**

> *To find the size of angle **SUT**, you will need to consider circle theorems.*

> *Begin by joining the point **O** to the points **T** and **R,** marking all the radiuses of the circle as equal lengths on the diagram.*

> *TP** and **TR **are also tangents to the circle, so by the circle theorem 'A tangent always meets a radius at 90°', angles **ORQ **and **OTP **are both 90°. *

$O \hat{R} Q = O \hat{T} P = 90^{\circ}$* **(angle between tangent and radius)*

**[1]**

> *Mark these onto the diagram.*

![QLY1pOQ2_4-8-edexcel-gcse-vh-q3-diagram-2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-maths-international-maths-23-extended/geometry/circle-theorems/assets/004-qly1poq2-4-8-edexcel-gcse-vh-q3-diagram-2.png)

> *The sum of the interior angles in any polygon can be found using the formula 180°(n - 2). *
*A regular pentagon has 5 equal interior angles, therefore these can be found using the formula *$\frac{180 ( 5 - 2 )}{5}$*.*

> * *$T \hat{P} Q = P \hat{Q} R = \frac{3 ( 180 )}{5} = 108^{\circ}$

> *Add these angles to the diagram.*

![4-8-edexcel-gcse-vh-q3-diagram-3](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-maths-international-maths-23-extended/geometry/circle-theorems/assets/005-4-8-edexcel-gcse-vh-q3-diagram-3.png)

> *PQROT  **is a pentagon, so the angle **ROT**  can be found by subtracting the other four angles from the sun of the angles in a pentagon.*

> *The sum of the interior angles in any polygon can be found using the formula 180°(n - 2).*

$R \hat{O} T + O \hat{T} P + T \hat{P} Q + P \hat{Q} R + Q \hat{R} O = 180 ( 5 - 2 )^{\circ} = 540^{\circ}$

> *Substitute in the angles you know to find angle **ROT**.*

$\begin{gathered} R \hat{O} T + 90^{\circ} + 90^{\circ} + 108^{\circ} + 108^{\circ} & = 540^{\circ} \\ R \hat{O} T + 396^{\circ} & = 540^{\circ} \\ R \hat{O} T & = 144^{\circ} \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

> *By the circle theorem, the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference, angle **ROT **is twice angle **RUT.*

$R \hat{O} T = 2 ( R \hat{U} T ) = 2 ( S \hat{U} T )$

$S \hat{U} T = \frac{R \hat{O} T}{2} = \frac{144}{2} = 72^{\circ}$

**[1]**

> *This proves that angle **TSU **is equal to angle **SUT **and so triangle **STU **is isosceles.*

**Therefore ****ST ****= ****UT **
**All reasons given clearly**** [1]**

The hexagonal numbers are an increasing sequence of numbers, with each number greater than the one before.

To test whether a number, $x$, is a hexagonal number or not, you can substitute it into the formula:

$\frac{1+\sqrt{8x+1}}{4}$

If the output is a positive integer, then it is a hexagonal number.

A hexagonal number, $H_{n}$, and its position value, $n$, satisfy this formula in the following way:

$\frac{1+\sqrt{8H_{n}+1}}{4}=n$

By making $H_{n}$ the subject, show that the formula for the $n$th term of a hexagonal number is given by

$H_{n}=2n^{2}-n$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Multiply both sides by 4*

$1+\sqrt{8H_{n}+1}=4n$

> *Subtract 1 from both sides*

$\sqrt{8H_{n}+1}=4n-1$

> *Square both sides*

$8 H_{n} + 1 = ( 4 n - 1 )^{2}$

**[1]**

> *Subtract 1 from both sides*

$8 H_{n} = ( 4 n - 1 )^{2} - 1$

> *Divide both sides by 8*

$H_{n} = \frac{( 4 n - 1 )^{2} - 1}{8}$

> *Expand the squared brackets*

$\begin{gathered} H_{n} & = \frac{( 4 n - 1 ) ( 4 n - 1 ) - 1}{8} \\ = \frac{16 n^{2} - 4 n - 4 n + 1 - 1}{8} \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

> *Simplify the numerator by collecting like terms*

$\begin{gathered} H_{n} & = \frac{16 n^{2} - 8 n}{8} \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

> *Simplify the fraction by cancelling a factor of 8 from each term*

$H_{n}=2n^{2}-n$** [1]**

$R_{n}=\frac{1}{2n^{2}-n}$

> *Note that the expression on the denominator is the *$n$*th term formula for *$H_{n}$

The diagram shows a shaded region $T$ formed by removing an equilateral triangle$PQR$from a regular hexagon $ABCDEF$.

The points $P$ and $Q$ lie on $AB$ such that $AB=1.5\times PQ$.

Given that the area of region $T$ is $72\sqrt{3}\mathrm{cm}^{2}$ work out the length of $PQ$.

......................................................$\mathrm{cm}$
parts.solutionMd:
> *The formula for a triangle is *$A=\frac{1}{2}ab\mathrm{sin}C$* where **a **and **b **are the lengths of two sides that form angle **C**.** *
*Let **x** denote the length **PQ**. Triangle **PQR** is an equilateral triangle so all the lengths are equal and all the angles are 60°. Find the area by substituting **a** = **x**, **b** = **x **and **C** = 60. Simplify the expression,*

`| Area of P Q R | = 1 half x x x x x sin ( 60 ) | | _ = 1 half x x x x x (sqrt( 3)/(2) | | _ = (sqrt( 3)/(4) x ^2 | |`

**[1]**

> *The length **PQ** = 1.5**x**.A regular hexagon is made up of 6 equilateral triangles. Find the area of the hexagon by finding substituting **a** = 1.5**x**, **b** = 1.5**x** and **C** = 60 into the formula and multiplying by 6.*

`| Area of A B C D E F | = 1 half x 1.5 x x 1.5 x x sin ( 60 ) x 6 | | _ = 1 half x 1.5 x x 1.5 x x (sqrt( 3)/(2) x 6 | | _ = (27 sqrt( 3)/(8) x ^2 | |`

**[1]**

> *Form an equation using the fact that the difference between the area of the triangle and the hexagon is equal to *$72\sqrt{3}$* cm*<sup>*2*</sup>*.*

$\begin{gathered} \frac{27 \sqrt{3} }{8} x^{2} - \frac{ \sqrt{3} }{4} x^{2} & = 72 \sqrt{3} \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

> *Divide both sides √3 and multiply both sides by 8. Then solve the equation to find **x **(which is a positive value so you can ignore the negative square root).*

$\begin{array}{ccc}27 x ^{2} - 2 x ^{2} & = 576 \\ 25 x ^{2} & = 576 \\ x ^{2} & = & \frac{576}{25} \\ x = & \sqrt{\frac{576}{25}} \\ x = & \frac{24}{5}\end{array}$

**The length of ****PQ**** is 4.8 cm ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:

A solid metal cone has radius 10 cm and height 36 cm.

i) Calculate the volume of this cone. [The volume, $V$, of a cone with radius $r$ and height $h$ is  $V=\frac{1}{3}πr^{2}h$.]

......................................... cm<sup>3</sup>[2]

ii) The cone is cut, parallel to its base, to give a smaller cone.

![cie-igcse-2018-oct-nov-p4-tz2-q10bii](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-maths-international-maths-23-extended/lengths-areas-and-volumes/circles-arcs-and-sectors/assets/023-cie-igcse-2018-oct-nov-p4-tz2-q10bii.png)

The volume of the smaller cone is half the volume of the original cone.
The smaller cone is melted down to make two different spheres.
The ratio of the radii of these two spheres is 1 : 2.

Calculate the radius of the smaller sphere.
[The volume, $V$, of a sphere with radius $r$ is  $V=\frac{4}{3}πr^{3}$.]

.......................................... cm [4]
parts.solutionMd:
i) *Find the volume of the cone by substituting *$r=10$* and *$h=36$* into the formula* * *

$\frac{1}{3}\timesπ\times10^{2}\times36$

**[1]**

> *Work out the value on your calculator, giving your answer to 3 significant figures*

**3770 cm**<sup>**3**</sup> **[1]**

ii) *Find the volume of the smaller cone by halving the volume of the bigger cone in part (b)(i)* * *

$\frac{1}{2}\times3770=1885$* cm**<sup>3</sup>*

**[1]**

*Method 1*  
*The ratio of radii (lengths) is 1 : 2 so the ratio of volumes is 1*<sup>*3*</sup>* : 2*<sup>*3*</sup>

*Split this volume up into the ratio 1 : 8 (by finding *$\frac{1}{9}$* of it and *$\frac{8}{9}$* of it)* * *

$\frac{1}{9}\times1885:\frac{8}{9}\times1885\,$ * *

*The volume of the smaller sphere is *$\frac{1}{9}\times1885$ 
*Form an equation in *$r$* by setting the sphere volume formula equal to *$\frac{1}{9}\times1885$ * *

$\frac{4}{3}πr^{3}=\frac{1}{9}\times1885$

**[2]**

*Get *$r^{3}$* on its own (by dividing both sides by *$\frac{4}{3}π$*)* * *

$r^{3}=\frac{\frac{1}{9}\times1885}{\frac{4}{3}π}\,$ * *

*Find *$r$* (by cube-rooting both sides)* * *

$r = cbrt( ( 1 / 9 x 1885 )/( 4 / 3 \pi ) )$

**3.68 cm*** ***[1]**

*Method 2* 
*The ratio of radii is 1: 2 so write the smaller sphere radius as *$r$* and the bigger sphere radius as *$2r$ 
*Form an equation in *$r$* (the sum of the volumes of the two spheres equals *$1885$*)* * *

$\frac{4}{3} \mathrm{\pi } r^{3} + \frac{4}{3} \mathrm{\pi } ( 2 r )^{3} = 1885$

**[1]**

*Collect like terms, using *$( 2 r )^{3} = 8 r^{3}$ * *

$\frac{4}{3}πr^{3}+\frac{4}{3}π\times8r^{3}=1885\,\frac{36}{3}πr^{3}=1885\,12πr^{3}=1885$ * *

*Find *$r$* (by dividing both sides by *$12π$* then cube-rooting)*

$r = \sqrt[3]{ \frac{1885}{12 \mathrm{\pi } } }$

**[1]**

**3.68 cm ****[1]**

The top of the cake is in the shape of a circle. 
The diameter of the circle is 7 inches.

A ribbon is going to be put around the side of the cake. Ribbons are sold in 50 cm lengths.

1 inch is 2.54 cm.

You must show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
> *The diameter of the cake is given in inches and the ribbon length is given in cm. Use the given ratio (1 inch = 2.54 cm) to convert the diameter of the cake into cm. *

$d_{( c m )} = 7 \times 2.54 \text{cm} = 17.78 \text{cm}$

**[1]**

> *To fit perfectly around the edge of the cake, the ribbon will be the length of the **circumference **of the circle.*

> *The formula for the circumference of a circle is *$2πr=πd.$* Use the *$π$* button on your calculator or "3.142", substituting 17.78 in for the diameter, **d.*

$C=π\times17.78=55.85751...$* *

**[1]**

> *One length of ribbon is 50 cm which is **less than **the circumference of the cake (55.857... cm).*

$55.85751...\mathrm{cm}>50\mathrm{cm}$

**[1]**

**No, one length of ribbon is not long enough to go around the cake ****[1] **
**Working must be shown for all marks.**

parts.solutionMd:
i) *A sector is a portion, or a fraction, of a circle*

> *The arc length will therefore be a fraction, out of 360°, of the circumference of a circle (*$2πr$*)*

> *In general, the length of an arc can be found by *

> $\mathrm{Arc} \mathrm{length}=\frac{θ}{360}\times2πr$* , where **θ** is the angle at the centre and **r** is the radius*

> *Applying this formula to the given sector*

$7.7=\frac{y}{360}\times2\timesπ\times3.8$

**[1]**

$2772=y\times2\timesπ\times3.8$

> *Divide both sides by *$( 2 \times \mathrm{\pi } \times 3.8 )$* (or 23.876... , but it is best to use accurate values)*

> *Evaluate using calculator*

$y=116.0993427...$

$y=116.1$ **[1]** 
**Round angles to 1 decimal place**

ii) *A sector is a portion, or a fraction, of a circle*

> *The area of a sector will therefore be a fraction, out of 360°, of the area of a circle (*$πr^{2}$*)*

> *In general, the area of a sector can be found by*

> $\mathrm{Area} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{sector}=\frac{θ}{360}\timesπr^{2}$* , where **θ** is the angle at the centre and **r** is the radius*

> *Applying this formula to the given sector, using the most accurate form of your answer from part i for the angle*

$\mathrm{Area}=\frac{116.0993427}{360}\timesπ\times3.8^{2}$

**[1]**

$\mathrm{Area}=14.63...$

$14.6\mathrm{cm}^{2}$* ***[1]*** *
**Rounded to 3 significant figures**

Cylinder $A$ has height 1.6 m and radius 0.56 m.

Cylinder $B$ is mathematically similar to cylinder $A$.
The height of cylinder $B$ is 0.6 m. 
Work out the radius of cylinder $B$.

....................................................... m
parts.solutionMd:
> *The radius of **A** and the radius of **B** are corresponding lengths in similar shapes so find **k, **the scale factor, using**  *$\begin{array}{rcl} k = \frac{second \text{corresponding} length}{first \text{corresponding} length} \end{array}$

> *Method 1*

> *The radius of **B** is smaller than the radius of **A**. **To go from the big shape to the small shape, put the small length on top in the fraction so that **k** will be smaller than 1*

$\begin{gathered} k & = \frac{height B}{height A} = \frac{0.6}{1.6} = \frac{3}{8} \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

> *Find radius of **B** by multiplying the radius of **A** by **k **(notice that **k** < 1 so multiplying by **k** will make the length smaller)*

$\begin{gathered} \text{radius} B & = k [ \text{radius} A ] = \frac{3}{8} \times 0.56 \end{gathered}$

**0.21 m**** ****[1]**

> *Method 2*

> *Finding **k **using**  *$\begin{array}{rcl} k = \frac{second \text{corresponding} length}{first \text{corresponding} length} \end{array}$*, if you put the larger length on top of the fraction then;*

$\begin{gathered} k & = \frac{height A}{height B} = \frac{1.6}{0.6} = \frac{8}{3} \end{gathered}$

> *Notice that **k** > 1 so multiplying by **k** will make the length bigger- but in going from the radius of **A** to the radius of **B**, we want to go from a longer length to a smaller length. So divide by **k **instead*

$\begin{gathered} \text{radius} B & = \text{radius} A \div k = 0.56 \div \frac{3}{8} \end{gathered}$

**0.21 m**** ****[1]**

> *Work out the length scale factor (LSF), by taking the cube root of the VSF.*

`LSF = cbrt( VSF LSF = cbrt( 27 / 8 ) LSF = 3 / 2`

**[1]**

> *Work out the area scale factor (ASF), by squaring the LSF.*

$\text{ASF} = LSF^{2}
\text{ASF} = ( \frac{3}{2} )^{2}
\text{ASF} = \frac{9}{4}$

> *Multiply the area of the smaller prism by the ASF to find the area of the larger prism.*

$36\times\frac{9}{4}$

**[1]**

**81 cm**<sup>**2**</sup>** ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:
*If two shapes are mathematically similar, their length, area and volume scale factors are **k**, **k*<sup>*2*</sup>* and **k*<sup>*3*</sup> 
*Find the area scale factor, from small-to-large (by dividing the large area by the small area)* * *

$k^{2}=\frac{226}{94}$ * *

*Find the length scale factor, **k**, by square-rooting both sides* * *

$k=\sqrt{\frac{226}{94}}$

**[1]**

*Find the volume scale factor, **k*<sup>*3*</sup>*, by cubing **k* * *

$k ^{3} = ( \sqrt{\frac{226}{94}} ) ^{3}$ * *

*This scale factor is how much bigger the larger container is compared to the smaller container* * *

*the larger volume, 680 cm**<sup>3</sup>**, is *$( \sqrt{\frac{226}{94}} ) ^{3}$* times bigger than the smaller volume* * *

*Find the smaller volume, by dividing the large volume by *$( \sqrt{\frac{226}{94}} ) ^{3}$ * *

*smaller volume = *$\frac{680}{open} \text{parentheses} \sqrt{\frac{226}{94}} ) ^{3}$

**[1]**

> *Use a calculator to find this value, giving your answer to 3 significant figures*

**182 cm**<sup>**3**</sup>** ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
A cone has height 15 cm and a base of radius 9 cm.

A smaller cone is cut off the top to form a frustum of height 11 cm.

![Diagram of a frustum, showing its formation from a cone. Includes measurements: diameter 9 cm, height 15 cm, labelled "Frustum".](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-maths-international-maths-23-extended/lengths-areas-and-volumes/congruence-and-similarity/assets/001-diagram-of-a-frustum-showing-its-formation-from-.png)

Find the exact volume of the frustum.
parts.solutionMd:
> *The volume of the frustum is equal to the volume of the large cone, subtract the volume of the smaller cone that has been removed*

> *The formula for the volume of a cone is given by *$V=\frac{1}{3}πr^{2}h$

> *Find the volume of the larger cone *$( V_{L} )$

$V_{L} = 1 \frac{1}{3} \pi ( 9^{2} ) ( 15 )
V_{L} = 405 \pi$

**[M1 A1]**

> *The smaller cone has a height of 15-11=4 cm*

> *The radius of the smaller cone is not known yet, but you can use similarity to find it*

> *Consider a cross section of the large cone and the small cone. You know the height of the small cone (4), the height of the large cone (15) and the radius of the large cone (9)*

![Two right-angled triangles; small one with height 4 cm, base r cm, large one with height 15 cm, base 9 cm; sides are proportional.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-maths-international-maths-23-extended/lengths-areas-and-volumes/congruence-and-similarity/assets/002-two-right-angled-triangles-small-one-with-height.png)

> *The triangles are similar; there is a constant scale factor for the side lengths*

$\begin{gathered} \frac{4}{15} & = \frac{r}{9} \\ \frac{4}{15} \times 9 & = r \\ 2.4 & = r \end{gathered}$

**[M1]**

> *Find the volume of the smaller cone *$( V_{S} )$

$V_{S} = 1 \frac{1}{3} \pi ( 2.4 )^{2} ( 4 )
V_{S} = \frac{192}{25} \pi$

**[A1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Alternatively, you could use a volume scale factor to find the smaller cone's volume:
> 
> $V_{S} = ( \frac{4}{15} )^{3} \times V_{L}$

> *The volume of the frustum is the volume of the larger cone subtract the volume of the smaller cone*

$V=V_{L}-V_{S}=405π-\frac{192}{25}π$

**[M1]**

$\frac{9933}{25}π$

**[A1]**

> 
> **A1**: Finding the volume of the larger cone. Can be implied by later working.
> 
> **M1**: Evidence of using similarity. Either to find the unknown radius or using a volume scale factor $( \frac{4}{15} )^{3}$.
> 
> **A1**: Finding the volume of the smaller cone. Can be implied by later working.
> 
> **M1**: Method to find the volume of the frustum.

parts.solutionMd:
> $AD$* is a diameter so the radius is half of *$AD$* Angle *$ACD$* is 90° because it is the angle in a semi-circle*

![cie-igcse-2020-may-jun-tz1-p2-q13](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-maths-international-maths-23-extended/lengths-areas-and-volumes/congruence-and-similarity/assets/023-cie-igcse-2020-may-jun-tz1-p2-q13.png)

> *Therefore *$AD$* is the hypotenuse of right-angle triangle *$ACD$*. We can use Pythagoras' theorem to find *$AD$* but we need to find *$AC$* first*

> *Triangle *$ABE$* and triangle *$ACD$* are similar, and the scale factor is:*

$\frac{\mathrm{equivalent} \mathrm{longer} \mathrm{side}}{\mathrm{equivalent} \mathrm{shorter} \mathrm{side}}=\frac{CD}{BE}=\frac{18}{13.5}$

**[1]**

> *Multiplying the length of *$AB$* by the scale factor gives *$AC$

**[1]**

> *Now we can use Pythagoras' theorem *$a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}$

$28^{2}+18^{2}=AD^{2}$

**[1]**

> *Rearrange to get *$AD$

$\begin{gathered} A D & = \sqrt{28^{2} + 18^{2}} \\ = 33.28663395 \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

> *The radius is half of *$AD$

$\begin{gathered} r = ( 33.28663395... ) \div 2 \\ = 16.64331698... \end{gathered}$

> *Round the answer to at least 3 significant figures*

**16.6 cm**** ****[1]**

parts.solutionMd:
> *When a shape is enlarged by a scale factor, the lengths are multiplied by the scale factor, and the area is multiplied by the (scale factor)*<sup>*2*</sup>*, also known as the area scale factor*

$3.5:1$

> *Rewriting with integers*

$7:2$ **[1]**

parts.solutionMd:
> *Find the volume of the smaller cone by halving the volume of the bigger cone in part (b)(i) *

$\frac{1}{2}\times3770=1885$* cm**<sup>3</sup>*

**[1]**

*Method 1* 
*The ratio of radii (lengths) is 1 : 2 so the ratio of volumes is 1*<sup>*3*</sup>* : 2*<sup>*3*</sup> 
*Split this volume up into the ratio 1 : 8 (by finding *$\frac{1}{9}$* of it and *$\frac{8}{9}$* of it*

> $\frac{1}{9}\times1885:\frac{8}{9}\times1885\,$* *

*The volume of the smaller sphere is *$\frac{1}{9}\times1885$

*Method 2*  
*The ratio of radii is 1: 2 so write the smaller sphere radius as *$r$* and the bigger sphere radius as *$2r$
 *Form an equation in *$r$* (the sum of the volumes of the two spheres equals *$1885$*)* * *

**[1]**

*Collect like terms, using *$( 2 r )^{3} = 8 r^{3}$ * *

$d=$ ......................................... cm [2]
parts.solutionMd:
i) *The volume of water needed will be the volume of the cylindrical tank minus the volume of the sphere.*

> *Find the volume of the cylindrical tank. *
*Formula for volume of a cylinder: *$V=πr^{2}h$*, where *$r$* is the radius and *$h$* is the depth of the tank.*

> * Substitute *$r=25$* and *$h=60$* into the formula. *

$\begin{gathered} V_{( \tan k )} & = \pi ( 25 )^{2} ( 60 ) \\ = 37500 \pi \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

> *Subtract the volume of the sphere from the volume of the tank. Using exact values for both is better practice and will give you the most accurate possible answer. *

$\begin{gathered} V_{( w a t e r )} & = V_{( t a n k )} - V_{( s p h e r e )} \\ = 37500 \pi - 4500 \pi \\ = 33000 \pi \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

> *Use your calculator to find the solution.  *

$\begin{gathered} V_{( water )} & = 33000 \pi = 103672.557... \end{gathered}$

$\begin{array}{ccc} V_{stretchy} ( water \text{stretchy} ) & = & 103700 cm^{ } 3\end{array}$ **[1]**
**Final mark awarded for any answer that rounds to this.**

ii) *The volume of the water has not changed so depth of the water can be found by modelling the volume of water found in part (i) as a cylinder and solving for the height.*

> * Formula for volume of a cylinder: *$V=πr^{2}h$*, where *$r$* is the radius and *$h$* is the depth of the water.*

> * Substitute *$r=25$* and *$V=33000π$*  into the formula. It is a good idea to leave your answer in terms of *$π$* for the next part of your calculation.*

> * *$\begin{gathered} V_{( water )} & = \pi r^{2} d \\ 33000 \pi & = ( 25 )^{2} \pi d \end{gathered}$

> * Cancel *$π$* from both sides of the equation.*

$\begin{gathered} 33000 = 625 d \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

> * Solve by dividing both sides by 625.*

$\begin{gathered} d & = \frac{ 33000}{625} = 52.8 \end{gathered}$

$\begin{gathered} d & = 52 . 8 \text{cm} \end{gathered}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
A cone has height 15 cm and a base of radius 9 cm.

A smaller cone is cut off the top to form a frustum of height 11 cm.

![Diagram of a frustum, showing its formation from a cone. Includes measurements: diameter 9 cm, height 15 cm, labelled "Frustum".](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-maths-international-maths-23-extended/lengths-areas-and-volumes/volume-and-surface-area/assets/001-diagram-of-a-frustum-showing-its-formation-from-.png)

Find the exact volume of the frustum.
parts.solutionMd:
> *The volume of the frustum is equal to the volume of the large cone, subtract the volume of the smaller cone that has been removed*

> *The formula for the volume of a cone is given by *$V=\frac{1}{3}πr^{2}h$

> *Find the volume of the larger cone *$( V_{L} )$

$V_{L} = 1 \frac{1}{3} \pi ( 9^{2} ) ( 15 )
V_{L} = 405 \pi$

**[M1 A1]**

> *The smaller cone has a height of 15-11=4 cm*

> *The radius of the smaller cone is not known yet, but you can use similarity to find it*

> *Consider a cross section of the large cone and the small cone. You know the height of the small cone (4), the height of the large cone (15) and the radius of the large cone (9)*

![Two right-angled triangles; small one with height 4 cm, base r cm, large one with height 15 cm, base 9 cm; sides are proportional.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-maths-international-maths-23-extended/lengths-areas-and-volumes/volume-and-surface-area/assets/002-two-right-angled-triangles-small-one-with-height.png)

> *The triangles are similar; there is a constant scale factor for the side lengths*

$\begin{gathered} \frac{4}{15} & = \frac{r}{9} \\ \frac{4}{15} \times 9 & = r \\ 2.4 & = r \end{gathered}$

**[M1]**

> *Find the volume of the smaller cone *$( V_{S} )$

$V_{S} = 1 \frac{1}{3} \pi ( 2.4 )^{2} ( 4 )
V_{S} = \frac{192}{25} \pi$

**[A1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Alternatively, you could use a volume scale factor to find the smaller cone's volume:
> 
> $V_{S} = ( \frac{4}{15} )^{3} \times V_{L}$

> *The volume of the frustum is the volume of the larger cone subtract the volume of the smaller cone*

$V=V_{L}-V_{S}=405π-\frac{192}{25}π$

**[M1]**

$\frac{9933}{25}π$

**[A1]**

*Bottom : 12 × 8 = 96*

parts.problemMd:
A cylinder with radius 6 cm and height $h$ cm has the same volume as a sphere with radius 4.5 cm.

Find the value of $h$.
 [The volume, $V$, of a sphere with radius $r$ is $V=\frac{4}{3}πr^{3}$.]

$h=$................................................
parts.solutionMd:
*The formula for the volume of a cylinder is *$V=πr^{2}h$* where **r** is the radius and **h** is the height.* 
*You know **r** = 6 so form an expression for the volume of the cylinder.*

$V=π\times6^{2}\times h$

> *Simplify the expression and leave it in terms of π.*

$V=36πh$

*The formula for the volume of a sphere is *$V=\frac{4}{3}πr^{3}$* where **r** is the radius.* 
*You know **r** = 4.5 so form an expression for the volume of the sphere.*

$V=\frac{4}{3}\timesπ\times4.5^{3}$

> *Simplify the expression and leave it in terms of π.*

$V=\frac{243}{2}π$

> *The cylinder and sphere have the same volume so make the expressions equal to each other.*

$36hπ=\frac{243}{2}π$

**[1]**

> *Both sides have a factor of π, so you can divide both sides by π to cancel it out.*

$36h=\frac{243}{2}$

> *Divide both sides by 36.*

$h = \frac{ ( \frac{243}{2} ) }{36} = \frac{27}{8}$

**[1]**

$h=3.375$ **[1]**

$r=$................................................
parts.solutionMd:
> *The volume of a cube is *$V=l^{3}$* where **l **is the length a side. *
*You know **l** = 20 so find the volume.*

$V=20^{3}=8000$

> *This is the volume of 40 spheres. Find the volume of one sphere by dividing by 40.*

$\frac{8000}{40}=200$

*The formula for the volume of a sphere is *$V=\frac{4}{3}πr^{3}$* where **r** is the radius.* 
*You know **V** = 200 so form an equation.*

$200=\frac{4}{3}πr^{3}$

**[1]**

> *Multiply both sides by 3 and divide both sides by 4.*

$πr^{3}=\frac{200\times3}{4}\,πr^{3}=150$

> *Divide both sides by π but leave as an exact expression.*

$r^{3}=\frac{150}{π}$

**[1]**

> *Cube root both sides.*

`r = cbrt( 150 / pi ) = 3.62783...`

> *Round to 3 significant figures.*

$r=3.63$ **[1]**

Give your answer in seconds, correct to the nearest second.

............................................. s
parts.solutionMd:
> *As the rate is stated in mm*<sup>*3*</sup>* per second, we should first change the volume of the salt, which is in cm*<sup>*3*</sup>*, to mm*<sup>*3*</sup>

> *1 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* is 1 cm × 1 cm × 1 cm, or 10 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm, so 1 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* = 1000 mm*<sup>*3*</sup>

$18.9\times1000=18900\mathrm{mm}^{3}$

**[1]**

> *Consider the units of 200 **mm*<sup>*3*</sup>* per second**, this is volume divided by (per) time*

$200 = \frac{volume ( \text{in} mm^{3} )}{time ( \text{in} \text{seconds} )}$

> *Filling in the known volume of the salt*

$200=\frac{18900}{\mathrm{time}}$

**[1]**

> *Multiply both sides by time, and then divide both sides by 200*

$\mathrm{time}=\frac{18900}{200}=94.5\mathrm{seconds}$

**95 s ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
![cie-igcse-2018-march-p4-q5a](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-maths-international-maths-23-extended/lengths-areas-and-volumes/volume-and-surface-area/assets/008-cie-igcse-2018-march-p4-q5a.png)

The diagram shows a solid prism with length 15.2 cm. The cross-section of this prism is a **regular** hexagon with side 7 cm.

Calculate the volume of the prism.

......................................... cm<sup>3</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
*Volume of a prism = cross-section area × length.* 
*We need to find the cross-section area, which is the area of the regular hexagon. Because the hexagon is regular, it can be split into 6 equilateral triangles as below.*

![cie-igcse-2018-march-p4-q5ai](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-maths-international-maths-23-extended/lengths-areas-and-volumes/volume-and-surface-area/assets/009-cie-igcse-2018-march-p4-q5ai.png)

> *As the triangles are equilateral, their internal angles are all 60° and the lengths are 7 cm. *
*We can use area of a triangle = *$\frac{1}{2}ab\mathrm{sin}C$* to find the area of one triangle.*

$\Delta \text{area} = 1 \frac{1}{2} \times 7 \times 7 \times \sin 60 ( = 21.21762239... )$

*Correct angle; 60°*** [1] **
*Rest of formula*** [1]**

> *And we can multiply this by 6 for the area of the hexagon.*

$\text{Hexagon} \text{area} = 6 \times 1 \frac{1}{2} \times 7 \times 7 \times \sin 60 ( = 127.3057344... )$

**[1]**

> *This (cross-sectional) area multiplied by the length 15.2 cm gives the volume.*

$\mathrm{Volume}=15.2\times6\times\frac{1}{2}\times7\times7\times\mathrm{sin}60$

**[1]**

$=1935.047162...$

**1935 cm**<sup>**3**</sup> **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The diagram shows a solid prism with length 15.2 cm. The cross-section of this prism is a regular hexagon with side 7 cm.

Calculate the total surface area of the prism.

......................................... cm<sup>2</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
> *Consider the net of a hexagonal prism.*

![5-c-a2eo_cie-igcse-2018-march-p4-q5aii](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-maths-international-maths-23-extended/lengths-areas-and-volumes/volume-and-surface-area/assets/010-5-c-a2eo-cie-igcse-2018-march-p4-q5aii.png)

*The surface area is made up of six identical rectangles and 2 identical hexagons.* 
*From part i) the area of one hexagon is*

$\text{Hexagon} \text{area} = 6 \times 1 \frac{1}{2} \times 7 \times 7 \times \sin 60 ( = 127.3057344... )$

> *Each rectangle has a width of 7 cm and a length of 15.2 cm.*

$\mathrm{Rectangle} \mathrm{area}=7\times15.2=106.4$

**[1]**

> *So the total surface area of the hexagonal prism is*

$\begin{gathered} \text{Surface} \text{area} & = 2 \times 127.305 734 ... + 6 \times 106.4 \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

$\begin{gathered} \text{Surface} \text{area} & = 254.611 468 ... + 638.4 \\ = 893.011 468 ... \end{gathered}$

**893 cm**<sup>**2**</sup> **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
A solid metal prism with volume 500 cm<sup>3</sup> is melted and made into 6 identical spheres.

Calculate the radius of each sphere. 
[The volume, $V$, of a sphere with radius $r$ is $V=\frac{4}{3}πr^{3}$.]

parts.solutionMd:

$500 \div 6 = 83. \dot{3} \text{or} \frac{250}{3}$

> *(It's a good idea to store the *$83. \dot{3}$* in your calculator, or use *$\frac{250}{3}$* to keep the final answer as accurate as possible).*

> *Substitute this volume into the given formula for the volume of a sphere.*

$\frac{250}{3}=\frac{4}{3}πr^{3}$

**[1]**

> *Rearrange and solve for *$r$*.*

`| 250 / 3 / 4 / 3 pi | = r ^3 | | r = cbrt( 250 / 3 / 4 / 3 pi ) | |`

**[1]**

$=2.709630351...$

**Answer = 2.71 cm** **[1]**

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:
> *Average speed is given by (total distance) ÷ (total time) *

*Average speed *$=\frac{400}{65}=6.153846154...$

$6.15$** ****m/s** **[1]**

**Give your answer to at least 3 significant figures**

parts.problemMd:

Work out the average speed of the train.

parts.solutionMd:
> *The required units is km/h so convert the time to hours.*

*6 hours and 39 minutes = 6.65 hours*

**[1]**

$\mathrm{Speed}=\frac{\mathrm{Distance}}{\mathrm{Time}}$*. If you forget this formula then it can be derived by looking at the units for speed km/h. Kilometres measure a distance and hours measure a time.* *Substitute 429 for the distance and 6.65 for the time.*

$\frac{429}{6.65}=64.5112...$

**[1]**

> *Round to one decimal place.*

**Speed is 64.5 km/h (1dp)** **[1]**

parts.problemMd:

Work out the average speed of the train.

...................................................... km/h
parts.solutionMd:
> *The required units is km/h so convert the time to hours.*

> *There are 60 minutes in an hour so divide 24 minutes by 60 to convert to hours.*

$\frac{24}{60}=0.4$

*3 hours and 24 minutes = 3.4 hours*

**[1]**

$\mathrm{Speed}=\frac{\mathrm{Distance}}{\mathrm{Time}}$*. If you forget this formula then it can be derived by looking at the units for speed km/h. Kilometres measure a distance and hours measure a time.* *Substitute 433.5 for the distance and 3.4 for the time.*

$\frac{433.5}{3.4}=127.5$

**[1]**

parts.problemMd:
A rocket travelled $100\mathrm{km}$ at an average speed of $28440\mathrm{km}/h.$

*Substitute 100 for the distance and 28440 for the speed.*

$28840=\frac{100}{\mathrm{Time}}$

> *Rearrange by multiplying both sides by Time and dividing both sides by 28840. Your answer will be in hours.*

$\mathrm{Time}=\frac{100}{28440}\mathrm{hours}$

**[1]**

> *There are 60 minutes in an hour and 60 seconds in each minute. Multiply by 60 twice to convert hours to seconds.*

$\begin{gathered} \frac{100}{28440} \times 60 \times 60 & = \frac{1000}{79} \\ = 12.6582... \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

> *Round to the nearest integer.*

**13 seconds (nearest second) ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Abelie flew by plane from Dubai to Rome.

The flight time was $6$ hours $42$ minutes. 
The average speed of the plane was $650$ kilometres per hour.

Work out the distance the plane flew.

..........................................kilometres
parts.solutionMd:
> *The given units are km/h so convert the time to hours.*

$\frac{42}{60}=0.7$

*6 hours and 42 minutes = 6.7 hours*

**[1]**

$\mathrm{Speed}=\frac{\mathrm{Distance}}{\mathrm{Time}}$*. If you forget this formula then it can be derived by looking at the units for speed km/h. Kilometres measure a distance and hours measure a time.* 
*Substitute 650 for the speed and 6.7 for the time.*

$650=\frac{\mathrm{Di}\text{stance}}{6.7}$

> *Multiply both sides by 6.7.*

$\mathrm{Distance}=650\times6.7$

**[1]**

**Distance is 4355 kilometres ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:

Find the pressure exerted by a force of 810 newtons on an area of 120 $\mathrm{cm}^{2}$

parts.solutionMd:

*120 cm**<sup>2</sup>** = 120 ÷ 10**<sup>4</sup>** cm**<sup>2</sup>** = 0.012 m**<sup>2</sup>*

**[1]**

> *Using the formula for pressure, substitute 810 for the force and 0.012 for the area.*

$\mathrm{Pressure}=\frac{810}{0.012}$

**[1]**

**Pressure is 67500 newtons/m**<sup>**2**</sup> **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Change a speed of 50 metres per second to a speed in kilometres per hour.

.......................... kilometres per hour
parts.solutionMd:
*Convert each unit separately.* 
*There are 60 seconds in a minute. Multiply by 60 to find how many metres are travelled in a minute.*

`| 50 metres per second | = 50 x 60 metres per minute | | _ = 3000 metres per minute | |`

**[1]**

> *There are 60 minutes in an hour. Multiply by 60 to find how many metres are travelled in an hour.*

`| 3000 metres per minute | = 3000 x 60 metres per hour | | _ = 180000 metres per hour | |`

> *There are 1000 metres in a kilometre. Divide by 1000 to find how many kilometres are travelled in an hour.*

$\begin{gathered} 18000 \text{metres} \text{per} \text{hour} & = \frac{180000}{1000} \text{kilometres} \text{per} \text{hour} \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

$180\mathrm{kilometres} \mathrm{per} \mathrm{hour}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd:

**[1]**

**472 km** **[1]**

parts.problemMd:

Calculate the distance the car travels.

$20$* seconds is *$20\div60=\frac{1}{3}$* minutes, which is  *$\frac{1}{3}\div60=\frac{1}{180}$*hours* * *

$108\times\frac{1}{180}=0.6$* km*

*Multiplying 108 by time* **[1]**

$0.6\times1000$* *

** [1]**

$600$** metres ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows a solid triangular prism.

![q5-1-11-easy-paper2-cie-igcse-maths-extended](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-maths-international-maths-23-extended/number/compound-measures-and-speed/assets/007-q5-1-11-easy-paper2-cie-igcse-maths-extended.png)

*The cross section here is a right-angled triangle with base 5 cm and height 12 cm. *
*For the area of that triangle, use  Area = (1/2) × Base × Height.  *

$\text{Volume} = ( 1 \frac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 12 ) \times 15 = 450 cm^{3}$

**[1]**

> *Each cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* has a mass of 6.6 grams. *
*So multiply 450 by 6.6 to find the mass of the prism.*

$450\times6.6=2970$

**[1]**

**2970 g****  [1]**

parts.problemMd:
A gold bar has a mass of 12.5 kg.

The density of gold is 19.3 g/cm<sup>3</sup>

Work out the volume of the gold bar. 
Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Density = Mass ÷ Volume  can be rearranged to give  Volume = Mass ÷ Density. *
*But be careful here!  The density is given in g/cm*<sup>*3*</sup>*, so 12.5 kg must first be converted to grams. *
*(Remember there are 1000 g in a kg.)*

$\begin{gathered} 12.5 \times 1000 & = 12500 \mathrm{g} \\ \\ 12500 \div 19.3 & = 647.668393... \end{gathered}$

**[2] **

> *1 mark for using Volume = Mass ÷ Density. *

> * 1 mark for converting kg to g.*

> *Round to 3 s.f. (and remember your units!).*

**648 cm**<sup>**3**</sup>**  [1]**
**Answers in range 647 to 648 will get the mark here.**

parts.problemMd:
Tame Valley is a company that makes yoghurt.

A machine fills trays of 20 pots with yoghurt. 
In one hour, the machine fills a total of 15 000 pots.

Work out how many seconds the machine takes to fill each tray of 20 pots.
parts.solutionMd:
> *We want the answer to be in seconds per tray. *
*Start by converting 1 hour into seconds. *
*Remember that there are 60 minutes in an hour, and 60 seconds in a minute.*

$1\mathrm{hour}=60\mathrm{minutes}=60\times60=3600\mathrm{seconds}$

**[1]**

> *Now divide 15000 by 20 to find how many trays are filled in an hour.*

$15000\div20=750\mathrm{trays} \mathrm{per} \mathrm{hour}$

**[1]**

> *Finally divide 3600 by 750 to find the number of seconds per tray.*

$3600\div750=4.8$

**[1]**

**4.8 seconds****  [1]**

parts.problemMd:
There are 18500 gallons of fuel in a fuel tank.

The fuel is pumped from the fuel tank into a plane at a rate of 1700 litres per minute.

1 gallon = 4.5 litres.

How many minutes will it take to empty the fuel tank completely? Give your answer to the nearest minute.
parts.solutionMd:

*Start by converting 18500 gallons into litres. *

$18500\times4.5=83250\mathrm{litres}$

**[1]**

> *And each minute, 1700 litres of fuel are pumped. So **divide** 83250 by 1700 to find the number of minutes.*

$83250\div1700=48.970588...\mathrm{minutes}$

**[1]**

> *Finally round to the nearest minute as asked for in the question.*

**49 minutes****  [1]**

> *Answers in the range 48.9 - 49.1 will get the mark here.*

parts.problemMd:

The wood has density $0.65\mathrm{kg}/m^{3}$

Work out the volume of the block of wood. 
Give your answer correct to $3$ significant figures.

*Substitute 0.65 for the density and 3.5 for the mass.*

$0.65=\frac{3.5}{\mathrm{Volume}}$

**[1]**

> *Multiply both sides by the volume and divide both sides by 0.65.*

$\begin{gathered} \text{Volume} = \frac{3.5}{0.65} \\ = \frac{70}{13} \\ = 5.384615... \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

> *Round to 3 significant figures. Your answer will be in cubic metres.*

**Volume is 5.38 m**<sup>**3**</sup>** (3sf)** **[1]**

parts.problemMd: Change a speed of $630$ kilometres per hour to a speed in metres per second.

**[1]**

> *There are 60 minutes in an hour. Divide by 60 to find how many kilometres are travelled in a second.*

$\begin{gathered} 10.5 \text{kilometres} \text{per} \text{minute} & = \frac{ 10.5 }{60} \text{kilometres} \text{per} \text{second} \\ = 0.175 \text{kilometres} \text{per} \text{second} \end{gathered}$

$\begin{array}{ccc}0.175 \text{kilometres} \text{per} \text{second} & = & 1000 \times 0.175 \text{metres} \text{per} \text{second} \end{array}$

**[1]**

$175\mathrm{metres} \mathrm{per} \mathrm{second}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
When the local time in Athens is 09 00, the local time in Berlin is 08 00. A plane leaves Athens at 13 15. It arrives in Berlin at 15 05 local time.

i) Find the flight time from Athens to Berlin.

........................ h ........................ min [1]

**2 h 50 mins ****[1]*** *

ii) *Speed = distance ÷ time.*

* **50 ÷ 60 = 0.833333....*
*2 + 0.833333..... = 2.833333.... hours*

* **Find the speed by dividing the distance travelled by the time taken.*

* **1802 ÷ 2.833333.... *

* Correct method** ***[1]**
**636 km/h ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
![cie-igcse-2020-may-june-p4-tz1-q7](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-maths-international-maths-23-extended/number/compound-measures-and-speed/assets/001-cie-igcse-2020-may-june-p4-tz1-q7.png)

The diagram shows the positions of three points $A$, $B$ and $C$ in a field. 
Mitchell takes 35 seconds to run from $A$ to $C$.

Calculate his average running speed in kilometres per hour.

........................................ km/h
parts.solutionMd:
> *The distance from **A** to **C** is 115 **metres.*
*The time taken is 35 **seconds**. *
*First convert the units to kilometres (1000 m = 1 km) and hours (1 hour = 3600 seconds (60 × 60)).*

$115 \mathrm{m} = \frac{115}{1000} = 0.115 \text{km}

**[1]**

$\begin{gathered} \frac{8 \times 11}{3 \times 4 } & = \frac{( 2 \times \cancel{2} \times \cancel{2} ) \times 11}{3 \times ( \cancel{2} \times \cancel{2} )} \\ = \frac{2 \times 11}{3} \\ = \frac{22}{3} \end{gathered}$

$2\frac{1}{3}=\frac{7}{3}$

**[1]**

> *Now we have *$\frac{7}{3}-\frac{7}{8}$* inside the bracket. *

> *The lowest common denominator of 3 and 8 is 24. So multiply the numerator and denominator of *$\frac{7}{3}$* by 8 and of *$\frac{7}{8}$* by 3*

$\frac{7}{3} - \frac{7}{8} 
( = \frac{7 \times 8}{3 \times 8} - \frac{7 \times 3}{8 \times 3} )
 = \frac{56}{24} - \frac{21}{24}$

**[1]**

> *Subtract the numerators*

$=\frac{35}{24}$

> *Now multiply *$\frac{35}{24}$* by *$\frac{6}{25}$*. *

> *Cancel diagonally first*

`( / 35 ^ 7)/( / 24 _ 4) x / 6 ^ 1 / / 25 _ 5 = 7 / 4 x 1 fifth`

*multiplying the two fractions ***[1]**

> *Then multiply across*

$\frac{7}{4}\times\frac{1}{5}=\frac{7\times1}{4\times5}$

> *Multiply across first*

$\frac{35}{24}\times\frac{6}{25}=\frac{210}{600}$

**Answer = **$\frac{7}{20}$** [1]**

parts.problemMd:

**[1]**

> *To subtract fractions you need a common denominator. 12 is the lowest common multiple of 4 and 12. *
*Convert the first fraction so that it also has a denominator of 12 by multiplying the numerator and denominator by 3.*

$\frac{7}{4}\times\frac{3}{3}=\frac{21}{12}$

**[1]**

> *Once the denominators are the same, you can then subtract the numerators.*

$\frac{21}{12}-\frac{11}{12}=\frac{10}{12}$

> *Simplify the fraction by cancelling out the highest common factor. The highest common factor of 10 and 12 is 2.*

$\frac{10}{12} = \frac{ \cancel{2} \times 5}{ \cancel{2} \times 6}$

$\frac{5}{6}$** ****[1]**

> *Method 2*

> *Subtract the whole numbers and the fractions separately.*

$1-0=1$

> *To subtract fractions you need a common denominator. 12 is the lowest common multiple of 4 and 12. *
*Convert the first fraction so that it also has a denominator of 12 by multiplying the numerator and denominator by 3.*

$\frac{3}{4}\times\frac{3}{3}=\frac{9}{12}$

**[1]**

> *Once the denominators are the same, you can then subtract the numerators.*

$\frac{9}{12}-\frac{11}{12}=-\frac{2}{12}$

$- \frac{2}{12} = - \frac{ \cancel{2} \times 1}{ \cancel{2} \times 6} = - \frac{1}{6}$

> *Combine the whole number and fraction.*

$1-\frac{1}{6}$

**[1]**

> *Subtract by converting the whole number to a fraction. Use the fact that *$1=\frac{6}{6}$*.*

$1-\frac{1}{6}=\frac{6}{6}-\frac{1}{6}=\frac{5}{6}$

parts.solutionMd:

> *The increase of 5% on the denominator is cubed, whilst the increase on the numerator is not, therefore the scale factor is less than 1 so **T **decreases.*

*The prime factors of 120 are 2, 2, 2, 3 and 5.*

parts.problemMd:
Arjun and Gretal each pay rent.

In 2018, the ratio of the amount each paid in rent was Arjun : Gretal = 5 : 7. 
In 2019, the ratio of the amount each paid in rent was Arjun : Gretal = 9 : 13.

Arjun paid the same amount of rent in both 2018 and 2019. 
Gretal paid \$290 more rent in 2019 than she did in 2018.

Work out the amount Arjun paid in rent in 2019.

\$ ................................................
parts.solutionMd:
> *First convert the ratios for each year and person to fractions out of the total rent.*

*In 2018, Arjun pays *$\frac{5}{5+7}=\frac{5}{12}$* of the total rent.  In 2019, Arjun pays *$\frac{9}{9+13}=\frac{9}{22}$* of the total rent.*

* In 2018, Greta pays *$\frac{7}{5+7}=\frac{7}{12}$* of the total rent.  In 2019, Greta pays *$\frac{13}{9+13}=\frac{13}{22}$* of the total rent.*

> *Letting **T*<sub>*1*</sub>* be the total rent paid in 2018 and **T*<sub>*2*</sub>* the total rent paid in 2019, we can write two equations in **T*<sub>*1*</sub>* and **T*<sub>*2*</sub>* using the given information. Arjun pays the same in 2018 and 2019:*

$\frac{9}{22}T_{2}=\frac{5}{12}T_{1}$

> *Greta pays \$290 more in 2019 than 2018:*

$\frac{13}{22}T_{2}=\frac{7}{12}T_{1}+290$

**[1]**

> *The question asks for Arjun's rent in 2019 so we only need to find **T*<sub>*2. *</sub>*Solve the two equations simultaneously, eliminating **T*<sub>*1*</sub>*. Rearrange the first equation to find **T*<sub>*1*</sub>* in terms of **T*<sub>*2*</sub>*.*

$T_{1}=\frac{9\times12}{22\times5}T_{2}=\frac{108}{110}T_{2}=\frac{54}{55}T_{2}$

> *Now substitute **T*<sub>*1*</sub>* into the second equation.*

$\therefore \frac{13}{22} T_{2} = \frac{7}{12} ( \frac{54}{55} T_{2} ) + 290$

**[1]**

> *Rearrange and solve for **T*<sub>*2*</sub>*.*

$\begin{gathered} \frac{13}{22} T_{2} - \frac{63}{110} T_{2} & = 290 \\ \frac{1}{55} T_{2} & = 290 \\ T_{2} & = 15 950 \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

> *In 2019, Arjun pays *$\frac{9}{22}$* of the total rent, so find the amount he pays by multiply this fraction by the total rent for 2019 (**T*<sub>*2*</sub>*).*

$\frac{9}{22}\times15950=6525$

**\$6525*** ***[1]**

**Whole number of US Dollars so two decimal places are not required.**

parts.solutionMd:

parts.problemMd: Expand and simplify $( 2 + \sqrt{3} )^{2} - ( 2 - \sqrt{3} )^{2}$.
parts.solutionMd:
*Method 1*

*Find (2 + √3)*<sup>*2*</sup>* (by multiplying 2 + √3 by itself)*

$\begin{gathered} ( 2 + \sqrt{3} ) ( 2 + \sqrt{3} ) & = 2 \times 2 + 2 \times \sqrt{3} + \sqrt{3} \times 2 + \sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{3} \end{gathered}$

*Simplify the terms (using the surd law *$\sqrt{a} \times \sqrt{a} = ( \sqrt{a} )^{2} = a$* for the last term) then collect like terms* * *

$\begin{gathered} = 4 + 2 \sqrt{3} + 2 \sqrt{3} + 3 \\ = 7 + 4 \sqrt{3} \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

> *Find (2 - √3)*<sup>*2*</sup>* (by multiplying 2 - √3 by itself) and do the same steps as above  *

$\begin{gathered} ( 2 - \sqrt{3} ) ( 2 - \sqrt{3} ) & = 2 \times 2 - 2 \times \sqrt{3} - \sqrt{3} \times 2 + \sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{3} \\ = 4 - 2 \sqrt{3} - 2 \sqrt{3} + 3 \\ = 7 - 4 \sqrt{3} \end{gathered}$

> *Find (2 + √3)*<sup>*2*</sup>* - (2 - √3)*<sup>*2*</sup>*  by subtracting the two results above (using brackets around the results) Collect like terms  *

$\begin{gathered} ( 2 + \sqrt{3} )^{2} - ( 2 - \sqrt{3} )^{2} & = ( 7 + 4 \sqrt{3} ) - ( 7 - 4 \sqrt{3} ) \\ = 7 + 4 \sqrt{3} - 7 + 4 \sqrt{3} \\ = 8 \sqrt{3} \end{gathered}$

$8\sqrt{3}$** *** ***[1]**

*Method 2*** **

> *Use the "difference of two squares" to factorise **a*<sup>*2*</sup>* - **b*<sup>*2*</sup>*  *

$a^{2} - b^{2} = ( a + b ) ( a - b )$

**[1]**

> *Substitute **a** = 2 + √3 and **b** = 2 - √3 into the expression and collect like terms  *

$\begin{array}{rcl} a^{2} - b^{2} & = ( 2 + \sqrt{3} + 2 - \sqrt{3} ) ( 2 + \sqrt{3} - ( 2 - \sqrt{3} ) ) \\ = ( 4 ) ( 2 + \sqrt{3} - 2 + \sqrt{3} ) \\ = 4 ( 2 \sqrt{3} ) \\ = 8 \sqrt{3} \end{array}$

$8\sqrt{3}$* ***[1]**

$\begin{gathered} \frac{14}{2 + \sqrt{3} } & = \frac{14 \times ( 2 - \sqrt{3} )}{( 2 + \sqrt{3} ) ( 2 - \sqrt{3} )} \\ \\ = \frac{28 - 14 \sqrt{3} }{4 + 2 \sqrt{3} - 2 \sqrt{3} + 3} \\ = \frac{28 - 14 \sqrt{3} }{7} \\ = 4 - 2 \sqrt{3} \end{gathered}$

Martin's answer is wrong.

Find Martin's mistake.
parts.solutionMd:
*He expanded the denominator incorrectly (the last term should be negative)*

`( 2 + sqrt( 3 ) ( 2 - sqrt( 3 ) = 4 + 2 sqrt( 3 - 2 sqrt( 3 bottom - 3`

parts.problemMd:
$a=\sqrt{8}+2\,b=\sqrt{8}-2\,T=a^{2}-b^{2}\,$

Work out the value of $T$.

Give your answer in the form $c\sqrt{2}$ where $c$ is an integer.
parts.solutionMd:
*Method 1*

*Find **a*<sup>*2*</sup>* (by multiplying √8 + 2 by itself)*

$\begin{gathered} a^{2} & = ( \sqrt{8} + 2 ) ( \sqrt{8} + 2 ) \\ = \sqrt{8} \times \sqrt{8} + \sqrt{8} \times 2 + 2 \times \sqrt{8} + 2 \times 2 \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

*Simplify the terms (using the surd law *$\sqrt{a} \times \sqrt{a} = ( \sqrt{a} )^{2} = a$* for the first term)* * *

$\begin{gathered} a^{2} & = 8 + 2 \sqrt{8} + 2 \sqrt{8} + 4 \\ = 12 + 4 \sqrt{8} \end{gathered}$ * *

> *Find **b*<sup>*2*</sup>* (by multiplying √8 - 2 by itself) and do the same steps as above  *

$\begin{gathered} b^{2} & = ( \sqrt{8} - 2 ) ( \sqrt{8} - 2 ) \\ = \sqrt{8} \times \sqrt{8} - \sqrt{8} \times 2 - 2 \times \sqrt{8} + 2 \times 2 \\ = 8 - 2 \sqrt{8} - 2 \sqrt{8} + 4 \\ = 12 - 4 \sqrt{8} \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

> *Find **a*<sup>*2*</sup>* - **b*<sup>*2*</sup>* by subtracting the two results above (using brackets around the results) Collect like terms  *

$\begin{gathered} a^{2} - b^{2} & = ( 12 + 4 \sqrt{8} ) - ( 12 - 4 \sqrt{8} ) \\ = 12 + 4 \sqrt{8} - 12 + 4 \sqrt{8} \\ = 8 \sqrt{8} \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

> *The result must be given in the form **c**√2 where** c** is an integer (whole number) Write *$\sqrt{8}$* as *$2\sqrt{2}$* (from *$\sqrt{8}=\sqrt{4\times2}=\sqrt{4}\sqrt{2}=2\sqrt{2}$*)  *

$\begin{gathered} a^{2} - b^{2} & = 8 \times 2 \sqrt{2} \\ = 16 \sqrt{2} \end{gathered}$

$16\sqrt{2}$** (where ****c**** = 16)*** ***[1]**

*Method 2*** **

> *Use the "difference of two squares" to factorise **a*<sup>*2*</sup>* - **b*<sup>*2*</sup>*  *

$a^{2} - b^{2} = ( a + b ) ( a - b )$

**[1]**

> *Substitute **a** = √8 + 2 and **b** = √8 - 2 into the expression and collect like terms  *

$\begin{array}{rcl} a^{2} - b^{2} & = ( \sqrt{8} + 2 + \sqrt{8} - 2 ) ( \sqrt{8} + 2 - ( \sqrt{8} - 2 ) ) \\ = ( 2 \sqrt{8} ) ( \sqrt{8} + 2 - \sqrt{8} + 2 ) \\ = ( 2 \sqrt{8} ) ( 4 ) \\ = 8 \sqrt{8} \end{array}$

**[1]**

> *The result must be given in the form **c**√2 where** c** is an integer (whole number) Write *$\sqrt{8}$* as *$2\sqrt{2}$* (from *$\sqrt{8}=\sqrt{4\times2}=\sqrt{4}\sqrt{2}=2\sqrt{2}$*)  *

$\begin{array}{rcl} a^{2} - b^{2} & = 8 \times 2 \sqrt{2} \end{array}$

**[1]**

> *Simplify the final answer (using 8 × 2 = 16)*

$16\sqrt{2}$** (where ****c**** = 16)*** ***[1]**

parts.problemMd: Show that  $\frac{6-\sqrt{8}}{\sqrt{2}-1}$    can be written in the form $a+b\sqrt{2}$  where $a$ and $b$ are integers.

**[1]**

> $\frac{6\sqrt{2}+6-\sqrt{16}-\sqrt{8}}{2-1}\,=\frac{6\sqrt{2}+6-4-\sqrt{8}}{1}\,=6\sqrt{2}+2-\sqrt{8}$*  *

parts.problemMd: Show that  $\frac{1}{1+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}$    can be written as  $2-\sqrt{2}$

*Method 1*

$\frac{1}{1 + \frac{1}{ \sqrt{2} }} \times \frac{ \sqrt{2} }{ \sqrt{2} }

$\frac{\sqrt{2}\times\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{2}\times1}{\sqrt{2}\times\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{2}\times1-1\times\sqrt{2}-1\times1}$ * *

> $\frac{2-\sqrt{2}}{2-1}\,=\frac{2-\sqrt{2}}{1}$*  *

> *The final answer is 2 - √2*

$2-\sqrt{2}$* ***[1]**

> *Method 2*

*Rationalise the denominator of *$\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$* (by multiplying top-and-bottom by √2)* *Use that √2 × √2 = 2* * *

$\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\times\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}}\,=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ * *

*Write out the fraction using this result* * *

$\frac{1}{1+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}}$

**[1]**

*Rationalise the denominator (by multiplying top-and-bottom by *$1-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$*)* *(Another way is to first multiply top-and-bottom by 2, then rationalise the denominator)* * *

$\frac{1}{( 1 + \frac{ \sqrt{2} }{2} )} \times \frac{( 1 - \frac{ \sqrt{2} }{2} )}{( 1 - \frac{ \sqrt{2} }{2} )}$

**[1]**

*Expand the denominator (for example, using the difference of two squares, (**a** + **b**)(**a** - **b**) = **a*<sup>*2*</sup>* - **b*<sup>*2*</sup>*)* * *

$\frac{1-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}}{1-\frac{2}{4}}\,=\frac{1-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}}{\frac{1}{2}}$ * *

*Dividing by a half is the same as multiplying by 2 (*$\div\frac{1}{2}$* means *$\times\frac{2}{1}$*)* * *

$= 2 ( 1 - \frac{ \sqrt{2} }{2} )
= 2 - \sqrt{2}$

$2-\sqrt{2}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd:

parts.problemMd:
In the following equation, $n$ is an integer greater than 1.

$( \sqrt{2} )^{n} = k \sqrt{2}$

i) Find $k$ when $n$ = 7.

$k$ = ...................... [2]

ii) Find $n$ when $k$ = 64.

$n$ = ..................... [2]
parts.solutionMd:
> *(i) When *$n=7$

$( \sqrt{2} )^{7} = k \sqrt{2}$

*Use the fact that *$( \sqrt{2} )^{2} = 2$* to help* *We can rewrite a power of 7 as a combination of powers of two using the law *$x^{y}\times x^{z}=x^{y+z}$

$\begin{gathered} ( \sqrt{2} )^{7} & = ( \sqrt{2} )^{2} \times ( \sqrt{2} )^{2} \times ( \sqrt{2} )^{2} \times ( \sqrt{2} )^{1} \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

> *Now simplify using *$( \sqrt{2} )^{2} = 2$

$\begin{gathered} ( \sqrt{2} )^{7} & = 2 \times 2 \times 2 \times ( \sqrt{2} )^{1} \\ ( \sqrt{2} )^{7} & = 8 \times \sqrt{2} \end{gathered}$

$k=8$ **[1]**

> *(ii) When *$k=64$

$( \sqrt{2} )^{n} = 64 \sqrt{2}$

> *We can use the fact that *$64=2^{6}$* to help*

$( \sqrt{2} )^{n} = 2^{6} \times \sqrt{2}$

*Use of 2*<sup>*6*</sup>* **[***1]**

> *Recall that *$\sqrt{2}=2^{\frac{1}{2}}$

$( \sqrt{2} )^{n = 2^{6} \times 2^{1} \frac{1}{2}}$

> *Use the law of indices *$x^{y}\times x^{z}=x^{y+z}$

$( \sqrt{2} )^{n = 2^{6.5} } = 2^{ \frac{13}{2} }$

> *We can now rewrite this in terms of *$\sqrt{2}$*, which is *$2^{\frac{1}{2}}$*, using the law *$( x^{y )^{z} = x^{y} z}$

$\begin{array}{ccc} ( \sqrt{2 ) ^{n}} & = & 2 ^{\frac{13}{2}} \\ ( \sqrt{2 ) ^{n}} & = & ( 2^{1} \text{half} ) ^{13} \\ ( \sqrt{2 ) ^{n}} & = & ( \sqrt{2 ) ^{13}}\end{array}$

$n=13$ **[1]**

**The official mark scheme also suggests using some trial and error for this question; trying different values of n and simplifying each time**

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:
> *Rewrite the mixed number as an improper fraction*

$2\frac{2}{9}=\frac{18}{9}+\frac{2}{9}=\frac{20}{9}$

> *Simplify *$\sqrt{80}$*, and note that when square-rooting a fraction, both the top and bottom are square-rooted*

$\sqrt{80}+\sqrt{\frac{20}{9}}=\sqrt{8}\sqrt{10}+\frac{\sqrt{20}}{\sqrt{9}}$

> *Simplify *$\sqrt{8}$*, *$\sqrt{20}$*, and *$\sqrt{9}$

$\sqrt{8}\sqrt{10}+\frac{\sqrt{20}}{\sqrt{9}}=\sqrt{4}\sqrt{2}\sqrt{10}+\frac{\sqrt{4}\sqrt{5}}{3}=2\sqrt{2}\sqrt{10}+\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{3}$

*Finding *$\sqrt{2\frac{2}{9}}=\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{3}$** [1]**

> *Combine the *$\sqrt{2}\sqrt{10}$* and simplify*

$2\sqrt{2}\sqrt{10}+\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{3}=2\sqrt{20}+\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{5}=2\sqrt{4}\sqrt{5}+\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{5}=2\times2\times\sqrt{5}+\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{5}=4\sqrt{5}+\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{5}$

*Finding *$\sqrt{80}=4\sqrt{5}$** [1]**

> *Combine the like-terms*

$4\sqrt{5}+\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{5}=\frac{12}{3}\sqrt{5}+\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{5}=\frac{14}{3}\sqrt{5}$

$\frac{14\sqrt{5}}{3}$* [1] *** **

**or equivalent e.g. **$\frac{28\sqrt{5}}{6}$

*The number of teachers at the school is unknown, so call it **N**. The probability of a teacher being male is 2/5. *
